entities.name: Sous vide
entities.fact: Sous vide cooks fish sealed in a bag in a water bath at a precisely controlled, low temperature.

entities.name: Confit
entities.fact: Confit cooks fish slowly in oil at a low temperature, and the result is very tender.

entities.name: Escabeche
entities.fact: Escabeche is a Spanish and Portuguese method in which fried or poached fish is preserved in a vinegar marinade.

entities.name: Citrus curing
entities.fact: Citrus curing soaks raw fish in lime or lemon juice, and the acid turns the flesh opaque as if it had been cooked.

entities.name: Cold smoking
entities.fact: Cold smoking flavours and preserves fish at low temperatures, below about 30 degrees Celsius, without cooking it, as in smoked salmon.

entities.name: Hot smoking
entities.fact: Hot smoking cooks fish at higher temperatures while smoking it, as with the Scottish Arbroath smokie.

entities.name: Kippering
entities.fact: Kippering splits a herring, soaks it in brine and cold smokes it, and the result is called a kipper.

entities.name: Teppanyaki
entities.fact: Teppanyaki is Japanese cooking on a flat iron griddle, often with seafood like prawns and scallops.

entities.name: Tataki
entities.fact: Tataki is a Japanese method of searing fish on the outside, leaving it raw inside, and slicing it, famously done with bonito.

entities.name: Fermenting
entities.fact: Fermenting preserves fish with salt and time, as in fish sauce, Swedish surstromming and Icelandic hakarl.

entities.name: Stockfish
entities.fact: Stockfish is unsalted cod dried on wooden racks in cold Arctic air, a Norwegian practice around the Lofoten Islands for centuries.

entities.name: Fish sauce
entities.fact: Fish sauce is made by fermenting small fish such as anchovies in salt, and the Romans made a similar condiment called garum.

entities.name: Matjes
entities.fact: Matjes is young, fat herring lightly salt-cured, a speciality of the Netherlands, Germany and Scandinavia.

entities.name: Lye soaking
entities.fact: Lye soaking rehydrates dried whitefish in an alkali solution, as in the Scandinavian dish lutefisk.

entities.name: Salt cod
entities.fact: Salt cod is cod that has been salted and dried so that it keeps for months, and it is the basis of Portuguese bacalhau dishes.

entities.name: Katsuobushi
entities.fact: Katsuobushi is skipjack tuna that has been cooked, smoked and fermented until as hard as wood, then shaved into flakes for Japanese stock.

entities.name: Himono
entities.fact: Himono is Japanese fish that is split, salted and dried, usually in the open air, before being grilled.

entities.name: Kusaya
entities.fact: Kusaya is a fermented and dried fish from Japan's Izu Islands, made in a brine that has been reused for generations.

entities.name: Pla ra
entities.fact: Pla ra is a Thai condiment of fish fermented with salt and rice bran for months.

entities.name: Bagoong
entities.fact: Bagoong is a Filipino paste of fermented fish or shrimp that is used as a seasoning or dip.

entities.name: Tinapa
entities.fact: Tinapa is Filipino fish, often milkfish, that is brined and smoked.

entities.name: Tsukudani
entities.fact: Tsukudani is a Japanese method of simmering small fish, shellfish or seaweed in soy sauce and mirin until they keep for a long time.

entities.name: Narezushi
entities.fact: Narezushi is the ancient form of sushi, in which fish is fermented for months with rice, and the rice was originally thrown away.

entities.name: Fisherman
entities.fact: Fishermen catch fish and shellfish at sea or on the coast, a job that is among the oldest in the world.

entities.name: Sailor
entities.fact: Sailors work aboard ships, handling lines, steering and keeping watch.

entities.name: Ship's captain
entities.fact: A ship's captain, also called the master, is the officer with ultimate command and legal responsibility for a vessel.

entities.name: Marine biologist
entities.fact: Marine biologists study life in the sea, from plankton to whales.

entities.name: Lifeguard
entities.fact: Lifeguards watch over swimmers on beaches and in the sea, and they train in rescue and first aid.

entities.name: Lighthouse keeper
entities.fact: Lighthouse keepers once tended the lamp and lived at remote towers, a role largely ended by automation in the twentieth century.

entities.name: Oceanographer
entities.fact: Oceanographers study the physical, chemical and biological workings of the ocean, including currents, waves and the seafloor.

entities.name: Harbour pilot
entities.fact: A harbour pilot is a local expert who boards a ship to guide it safely into and out of port.

entities.name: Scuba diver
entities.fact: Professional divers work underwater on tasks such as inspection, construction, salvage and research.

entities.name: Deckhand
entities.fact: A deckhand is a crew member who handles ropes, cargo and maintenance on a ship's deck.

entities.name: First mate
entities.fact: The first mate is the captain's second-in-command, and he or she often runs the ship's deck crew.

entities.name: Navigator
entities.fact: A navigator plots a ship's position and course, once with stars and a sextant, today often with satellite systems.

entities.name: Boatswain
entities.fact: The boatswain, pronounced bosun, supervises the deck crew and looks after the ship's rigging, anchors and boats.

entities.name: Ship's cook
entities.fact: The ship's cook prepares the crew's meals in the galley and is vital to morale on a long voyage.

entities.name: Harbour master
entities.fact: A harbour master oversees the safe movement of vessels in a port and enforces its rules.

entities.name: Coastguard
entities.fact: Coastguards patrol coastal waters and run search and rescue, and they enforce maritime law.

entities.name: Lobsterman
entities.fact: Lobstermen set baited traps called pots on the seabed to catch lobsters, especially around New England and Maine.

entities.name: Stevedore
entities.fact: Stevedores load and unload cargo from ships in port.

entities.name: Shipwright
entities.fact: A shipwright builds and repairs wooden ships and boats.

entities.name: Fishmonger
entities.fact: A fishmonger sells fresh fish and shellfish, often buying from local boats or markets.

entities.name: Marine engineer
entities.fact: A marine engineer runs and maintains a ship's engines and machinery.

entities.name: Naval architect
entities.fact: A naval architect designs ships and boats, working out their shape, strength and stability.

entities.name: Quartermaster
entities.fact: On a ship the quartermaster steers and helps with navigation, and in the navy the rank also covers stores and signals.

entities.name: Helmsman
entities.fact: A helmsman is the sailor who steers the ship.

entities.name: Purser
entities.fact: The purser is the ship's officer who manages money, passengers and supplies.

entities.name: Ship's surgeon
entities.fact: A ship's surgeon looked after the health of a ship's crew, and in naval history he was often also the ship's naturalist.

entities.name: Stoker
entities.fact: A stoker shovelled coal into the boilers of a steamship, working in hot and dirty conditions below decks.

entities.name: Sailmaker
entities.fact: A sailmaker cuts and sews sails, and in the age of sail every large ship carried one.

entities.name: Ship chandler
entities.fact: A ship chandler supplies provisions and equipment, such as rope, paint and lamps, to ships in port.

entities.name: Hydrographer
entities.fact: Hydrographers survey and map the seabed and coasts so that nautical charts are accurate.

entities.name: Marine geologist
entities.fact: Marine geologists study the rocks, sediments and structure of the ocean floor.

entities.name: Marine archaeologist
entities.fact: Marine archaeologists excavate and study shipwrecks and drowned settlements.

entities.name: Pearl diver
entities.fact: Pearl divers gather oysters from the seabed by free-diving, hunting for natural pearls.

entities.name: Oyster farmer
entities.fact: Oyster farmers raise oysters in beds or racks in coastal waters until they are ready to eat.

entities.name: Coxswain
entities.fact: A coxswain steers a small boat, a role in lifeboats and rowing crews that also includes command of the crew.

entities.name: Ship's carpenter
entities.fact: The ship's carpenter was responsible for the hull and masts, plugging leaks and mending damage in the age of sail.

entities.name: Cooper
entities.fact: A cooper makes the barrels used on ships to carry water, salted meat and other provisions.

entities.name: Rigger
entities.fact: A rigger fits and maintains the ropes and spars of a sailing ship, working high above the deck.

entities.name: Topman
entities.fact: A topman was a sailor stationed aloft to handle the upper sails of a square-rigged ship.

entities.name: Cabin boy
entities.fact: A cabin boy was a young servant who ran errands and waited on the officers aboard a ship.

entities.name: Powder monkey
entities.fact: A powder monkey was a young boy on a warship who carried gunpowder from the magazine to the cannon.

entities.name: Supercargo
entities.fact: A supercargo was the merchant's representative aboard a trading ship, in charge of the cargo and its sale.

entities.name: Harpooner
entities.fact: A harpooner threw the harpoon at a whale, and on a whaleship he was an officer in the whaleboat crew.

entities.name: Trawlerman
entities.fact: A trawlerman fishes by dragging a net behind a trawler, often on long voyages to distant fishing grounds.

entities.name: Shipbreaker
entities.fact: Shipbreakers take apart old ships to recycle the steel, much of it done on beaches in South Asia.

entities.name: Underwater welder
entities.fact: Underwater welders join and repair metal structures like pipelines and oil rigs beneath the sea.

entities.name: Saturation diver
entities.fact: Saturation divers live in pressurised chambers for weeks so they can work at great depth without repeated decompression.

entities.name: ROV pilot
entities.fact: An ROV pilot flies a remotely operated underwater vehicle, a tethered robot used for survey, inspection and research.

entities.name: Marine mammal trainer
entities.fact: Marine mammal trainers work with dolphins, seals and other sea mammals in aquariums and research programmes.

entities.name: Sponge diver
entities.fact: Sponge divers harvested natural sponges from the seabed, a tradition centred on Greece and Florida.

entities.name: Seaweed farmer
entities.fact: Seaweed farmers grow kelp and other seaweeds on ropes or nets in coastal waters.

entities.name: Ferryman
entities.fact: A ferryman carries passengers and goods across stretches of water by boat.

entities.name: Ama diver
entities.fact: Ama are Japanese women, historically, who free-dive without breathing apparatus to gather shellfish, seaweed and pearl oysters, a tradition that has lasted for well over a thousand years.

entities.name: Compass
entities.fact: A magnetic compass has a needle that aligns with the Earth's magnetic field, and Chinese and European sailors used it to steer for centuries.

entities.name: Sextant
entities.fact: A sextant measures the angle between a celestial body and the horizon, letting a navigator work out latitude.

entities.name: Sonar
entities.fact: Sonar uses sound pulses and their echoes to detect objects and map the seabed underwater.

entities.name: Radar
entities.fact: Radar bounces radio waves off objects, and ships use it to spot other vessels, land and storms in the dark or in fog.

entities.name: Knot
entities.fact: A knot is a speed of one nautical mile per hour, about 1.85 kilometres per hour.

entities.name: Fathom
entities.fact: A fathom is six feet, about 1.8 metres, and sailors used it to measure the depth of water.

entities.name: Nautical mile
entities.fact: A nautical mile is 1,852 metres, roughly one minute of latitude, and it is used for distances at sea.

entities.name: Astrolabe
entities.fact: The mariner's astrolabe was a simple brass instrument used from the fifteenth century to measure the height of the sun or stars at sea.

entities.name: Marine chronometer
entities.fact: The marine chronometer is a very accurate clock that lets navigators find longitude, and John Harrison perfected one in the eighteenth century.

entities.name: Barometer
entities.fact: A barometer measures air pressure, and a falling reading warns sailors that a storm may be coming.

entities.name: Binoculars
entities.fact: Binoculars are a pair of linked telescopes that sailors use to spot buoys, coastlines and other ships.

entities.name: GPS
entities.fact: The Global Positioning System uses signals from satellites to tell a ship its position almost anywhere on Earth.

entities.name: Echo sounder
entities.fact: An echo sounder measures water depth by timing how long a sound pulse takes to bounce off the seabed.

entities.name: Remotely operated vehicle
entities.fact: A remotely operated vehicle is an unmanned underwater robot linked to a ship by a cable and used to explore and work at depth.

entities.name: Spyglass
entities.fact: A spyglass is a small hand-held telescope, once a standard tool for watching distant ships and coasts.

entities.name: Anemometer
entities.fact: An anemometer measures wind speed, and sailors use it to judge how much sail to carry.

entities.name: Depth gauge
entities.fact: A depth gauge shows a diver how deep they are, which they use to avoid the dangers of excessive depth and pressure.

entities.name: Hydrophone
entities.fact: A hydrophone is an underwater microphone used to record whales, ships and other sounds in the sea.

entities.name: Plankton net
entities.fact: A plankton net is a fine mesh net towed through the sea to collect tiny drifting organisms for study.

entities.name: Quadrant
entities.fact: A quadrant measures the angle of a star or the sun above the horizon, and it was an early navigation tool used before the sextant.

entities.name: Secchi disk
entities.fact: A Secchi disk is a white disc lowered into the sea until it disappears from sight, which measures how clear the water is.

entities.name: Niskin bottle
entities.fact: A Niskin bottle is a tube that closes at both ends at a chosen depth to collect a water sample.

entities.name: CTD
entities.fact: A CTD is an instrument package that measures the conductivity, temperature and depth of seawater as it is lowered from a research ship.

entities.name: Lead line
entities.fact: A lead line is a weighted rope marked in fathoms that sailors dropped to measure depth and sample the seabed.

entities.name: Chip log
entities.fact: A chip log is a piece of wood thrown overboard on a knotted line to measure a ship's speed, which is the origin of the knot.

entities.name: Octant
entities.fact: The octant was an eighteenth-century navigation instrument that measured angles using mirrors and was the forerunner of the sextant.

entities.name: Backstaff
entities.fact: The backstaff let navigators measure the sun's height with their back to it, so they did not have to look into its glare.

entities.name: Side-scan sonar
entities.fact: Side-scan sonar is towed behind a ship and sends sound sideways to build images of the seabed, and it is often used to find wrecks.

entities.name: Multibeam echosounder
entities.fact: A multibeam echosounder sends a fan of sound beams beneath a ship to map a wide strip of the seabed at once.

entities.name: Tide gauge
entities.fact: A tide gauge records the rise and fall of the sea level at a harbour or coast.

entities.name: Argo float
entities.fact: Argo floats are robotic probes that drift with ocean currents, rising and sinking to measure temperature and salinity worldwide.

entities.name: Beaufort scale
entities.fact: The Beaufort scale rates wind strength from calm to hurricane, from 0 to 12, based on the effect on the sea and on sails.

entities.name: League
entities.fact: A league is an old unit of distance, about three nautical miles at sea, which is why Jules Verne's novel measures twenty thousand of them.

entities.name: Cable
entities.fact: A cable is a nautical unit of distance equal to a tenth of a nautical mile, or about 185 metres.

entities.name: Kamal
entities.fact: The kamal is a simple Arab navigation tool of a card on a knotted string, used to find latitude from the height of a star.

entities.name: Pelorus
entities.fact: A pelorus is a compass-like ring with sighting vanes that measures the bearing of an object relative to the ship's heading.

entities.name: Bathythermograph
entities.fact: A bathythermograph records the temperature of seawater at different depths as it descends.

entities.name: Piston corer
entities.fact: A piston corer is a long tube driven into the seabed to extract a column of sediment recording the history of the ocean.

entities.name: Plimsoll line
entities.fact: The Plimsoll line is a mark on a ship's hull showing the deepest it may safely be loaded, named after Samuel Plimsoll.

entities.name: Sverdrup
entities.fact: The sverdrup is the unit used for ocean currents, equal to one million cubic metres of water moving each second.

entities.name: EPIRB
entities.fact: An EPIRB is a beacon that sends a distress signal and position to satellites when a vessel sinks or the beacon gets wet.

entities.name: Automatic identification system
entities.fact: The automatic identification system broadcasts a ship's name, position and course so that other vessels and coastal stations can track it.

entities.name: Current meter
entities.fact: A current meter measures the speed and direction of water flow, either from a mooring or lowered from a ship.

entities.name: Sediment trap
entities.fact: A sediment trap is a funnel moored in the sea that collects the marine snow falling to the deep.

entities.name: Gyrocompass
entities.fact: A gyrocompass uses a fast-spinning gyroscope to find true north, so it is not thrown off by a ship's metal or magnetic fields.

entities.name: Cross-staff
entities.fact: The cross-staff was a medieval and Renaissance tool with a sliding crosspiece used to measure the angle of the sun or Pole Star.

entities.name: Traverse board
entities.fact: A traverse board was a peg board on which sailors recorded the courses and times of each half-hour watch for dead reckoning.

entities.name: Nocturnal
entities.fact: A nocturnal was a medieval tool that used the position of stars near the Pole Star to tell the time at night.

entities.name: Ocean bottom seismometer
entities.fact: An ocean bottom seismometer sits on the seabed to record earthquakes, from nearby tremors to those on the other side of the world.

entities.name: Manta trawl
entities.fact: A manta trawl is a net with a wide mouth towed along the sea surface to collect floating microplastics.

entities.name: Stick chart
entities.fact: The stick charts of the Marshall Islands were made of palm ribs and shells to represent the way ocean swells bend around islands, and navigators learned them on land.

entities.name: Port
entities.fact: Port is the left-hand side of a ship when facing forward, and the word replaced larboard to avoid confusion with starboard.

entities.name: Starboard
entities.fact: Starboard is the right-hand side of a ship when facing forward, from the old steering-board that was fixed on that side.

entities.name: Bow
entities.fact: The bow is the front of a ship or boat.

entities.name: Stern
entities.fact: The stern is the back of a ship or boat.

entities.name: Mast
entities.fact: A mast is the tall vertical pole that holds up a ship's sails and rigging.

entities.name: Anchor
entities.fact: An anchor is a heavy hook-shaped weight lowered to the seabed to hold a ship in place.

entities.name: Ahoy
entities.fact: Ahoy is a sailor's call to attract attention or hail another ship, and Alexander Graham Bell suggested it as a telephone greeting.

entities.name: Galley (kitchen)
entities.fact: The galley is a ship's kitchen, and the word also names an old kind of oared ship.

entities.name: Helm
entities.fact: The helm is the steering gear of a ship, meaning its wheel or tiller.

entities.name: Keel
entities.fact: The keel is the long structural beam along the bottom of a ship's hull, which keeps the vessel stable.

entities.name: Hull
entities.fact: The hull is the main body of a ship, the shell that keeps it afloat.

entities.name: Rudder
entities.fact: The rudder is the movable blade at the stern that steers the ship.

entities.name: Boom
entities.fact: The boom is the horizontal pole that holds the bottom edge of a sail.

entities.name: Jib
entities.fact: The jib is the triangular sail at the front of a sailing boat.

entities.name: Rigging
entities.fact: Rigging is the system of ropes, wires and chains that supports a ship's masts and controls its sails.

entities.name: Bilge
entities.fact: The bilge is the lowest part of a ship's interior, where water collects, and it is the source of the slang word for nonsense.

entities.name: Crow's nest
entities.fact: The crow's nest is a lookout platform high on a ship's mast.

entities.name: Aft
entities.fact: Aft means towards the back or stern of a ship.

entities.name: Forecastle
entities.fact: The forecastle, often written fo'c'sle, is the forward part of a ship where the crew traditionally lived.

entities.name: Poop deck
entities.fact: The poop deck is a raised deck at the stern of a ship, and the name comes from the Latin word for stern.

entities.name: Gangway
entities.fact: The gangway is the narrow walkway or ramp used to board and leave a ship.

entities.name: Halyard
entities.fact: A halyard is a rope used to hoist a sail or flag.

entities.name: Tiller
entities.fact: A tiller is a lever attached to the rudder, used to steer small boats.

entities.name: Bulkhead
entities.fact: A bulkhead is an upright wall inside a ship that divides it into compartments, which helps to contain flooding.

entities.name: Bollard
entities.fact: A bollard is a short, strong post on a quay or ship used to secure mooring ropes.

entities.name: Cleat
entities.fact: A cleat is a fitting to which a rope is tied off on a boat.

entities.name: Capstan
entities.fact: A capstan is a rotating drum used to haul in an anchor cable or heavy rope, and sailors once turned it by walking round with bars.

entities.name: Windlass
entities.fact: A windlass is a winch used on a ship to raise the anchor.

entities.name: Binnacle
entities.fact: A binnacle is the stand that holds a ship's compass near the helm.

entities.name: Gunwale
entities.fact: The gunwale, pronounced gunnel, is the upper edge of the side of a boat.

entities.name: Transom
entities.fact: The transom is the flat surface across the stern of a boat.

entities.name: Davit
entities.fact: A davit is a small crane on a ship's side used to lower and raise lifeboats.

entities.name: Scupper
entities.fact: A scupper is an opening in the side of a ship that lets water drain off the deck.

entities.name: Hawser
entities.fact: A hawser is a thick rope or cable used for mooring or towing a ship.

entities.name: Spinnaker
entities.fact: A spinnaker is a large balloon-like sail used for sailing downwind.

entities.name: Mizzen
entities.fact: The mizzen is the mast behind the main mast on a ship with two or more masts, and the sail set on it.

entities.name: Bowsprit
entities.fact: The bowsprit is a spar that projects forward from a ship's bow and supports the stays of the foremast.

entities.name: Taffrail
entities.fact: The taffrail is the rail around the stern of a ship, and a ship's log was often streamed from here.

entities.name: Stanchion
entities.fact: A stanchion is an upright post that supports a rail or an awning on a ship's deck.

entities.name: Thwart
entities.fact: A thwart is a seat across a small boat that also strengthens the hull.

entities.name: Painter
entities.fact: The painter is the rope attached to the bow of a small boat, used to tie it up.

entities.name: Marlinspike
entities.fact: A marlinspike is a pointed metal tool used by sailors to open the strands of rope for splicing.

entities.name: Luff
entities.fact: The luff is the forward edge of a sail, and to luff means to turn a sailing boat into the wind so that its sails flap.

entities.name: Cringle
entities.fact: A cringle is a rope loop or metal ring sewn into the edge of a sail for attaching lines.

entities.name: Clew
entities.fact: The clew is the lower back corner of a sail, where the sheets are attached.

entities.name: Kedge
entities.fact: A kedge is a light anchor used to pull a ship through a narrow channel or off the shore, and to kedge means to move a ship this way.

entities.name: Dogwatch
entities.fact: The dogwatches are the two short two-hour watches between 4 and 8 in the evening, which let crews rotate their duty hours.

entities.name: Landlubber
entities.fact: A landlubber is the sailors' term for someone who is inexperienced at sea.

entities.name: Avast
entities.fact: Avast is a sailor's command to stop or hold still, and it comes from the Dutch word houd vast.

entities.name: Grog
entities.fact: Grog was the daily rum ration mixed with water that was given to sailors in the Royal Navy from 1740 until 1970.

entities.name: Keelhaul
entities.fact: To keelhaul was a naval punishment of dragging a sailor under a ship's keel, and it is now used to mean being severely reprimanded.

entities.name: Doldrums
entities.fact: The doldrums are a belt of light winds near the equator that could leave sailing ships stuck for days.

entities.name: Scuttlebutt
entities.fact: The scuttlebutt was the cask of drinking water on a ship, where sailors gathered and gossiped, so the word came to mean rumour.

entities.name: Tide
entities.fact: Tides are the regular rise and fall of the sea, caused mainly by the gravity of the Moon and the Sun.

entities.name: Wave
entities.fact: Most ocean waves are made by wind blowing over the water surface, and bigger waves come from stronger wind blowing for longer.

entities.name: Tsunami
entities.fact: A tsunami is a series of enormous waves, usually triggered by an undersea earthquake, landslide or volcanic eruption.

entities.name: Ocean current
entities.fact: An ocean current is a continuous, directed flow of seawater, driven by wind, temperature and salinity differences.

entities.name: Whirlpool
entities.fact: A whirlpool is a rotating body of water, typically formed where opposing currents meet.

entities.name: El Nino
entities.fact: El Nino is a periodic warming of the eastern Pacific Ocean that changes weather patterns around the world.

entities.name: Rip current
entities.fact: A rip current is a narrow, fast channel of water flowing away from the shore, and it is a leading danger to swimmers.

entities.name: Bioluminescence
entities.fact: Bioluminescence is light produced by living organisms, and it makes the sea glow where plankton like dinoflagellates are disturbed.

entities.name: Hurricane
entities.fact: Hurricanes are intense tropical storms that gather energy from warm ocean water, and they are called typhoons in the western Pacific.

entities.name: Storm surge
entities.fact: A storm surge is a rise in sea level pushed onto the coast by the winds and low pressure of a storm.

entities.name: La Nina
entities.fact: La Nina is the cool phase of the Pacific climate cycle, when the eastern Pacific becomes unusually cold.

entities.name: Upwelling
entities.fact: Upwelling brings cold, nutrient-rich water from the deep to the surface, and it supports some of the world's richest fisheries.

entities.name: Spring tide
entities.fact: Spring tides are the highest and lowest tides, which occur around the new and full Moon when the Sun and Moon pull together.

entities.name: Neap tide
entities.fact: Neap tides are the smallest tides, which occur at the first and last quarter of the Moon.

entities.name: Maelstrom
entities.fact: A maelstrom is a powerful whirlpool, and the word comes from Dutch and was long linked to the tidal currents off northern Norway.

entities.name: Rogue wave
entities.fact: A rogue wave is an unusually large and unexpected wave, more than twice the height of the surrounding waves.

entities.name: Red tide
entities.fact: A red tide is a bloom of algae that colours the water and can poison fish and shellfish.

entities.name: Coral bleaching
entities.fact: Coral bleaching happens when warm water stresses corals into expelling the algae that give them colour and food.

entities.name: Waterspout
entities.fact: A waterspout is a spinning column of air and water vapour that forms over the sea, like a tornado over water.

entities.name: Tidal bore
entities.fact: A tidal bore is a wave that travels up a river against the current when a rising tide pushes into a narrowing estuary.

entities.name: King tide
entities.fact: A king tide is an especially high tide that occurs when the Moon is closest to Earth at new or full Moon.

entities.name: Sea fog
entities.fact: Sea fog forms when warm moist air moves over cold water, and it is common off coasts like California and Newfoundland.

entities.name: Thermohaline circulation
entities.fact: The thermohaline circulation is the global flow of ocean water driven by differences in temperature and salt content, which takes about a thousand years to complete.

entities.name: Ocean acidification
entities.fact: Ocean acidification is the fall in the sea's pH as it absorbs carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, which harms shell-building animals.

entities.name: Ocean gyre
entities.fact: An ocean gyre is a huge system of rotating currents, such as the North Pacific Gyre where floating rubbish gathers.

entities.name: Ocean eddy
entities.fact: An ocean eddy is a swirling loop of water that breaks off from a current and can carry heat and marine life across the sea.

entities.name: Algal bloom
entities.fact: An algal bloom is a rapid growth of algae or phytoplankton in the water, sometimes visible from space.

entities.name: Marine heatwave
entities.fact: A marine heatwave is a long period of unusually warm sea temperatures that can kill kelp, corals and fish.

entities.name: Swell
entities.fact: Swell consists of long, regular waves that have travelled out of the storm that made them, sometimes for thousands of miles.

entities.name: Longshore drift
entities.fact: Longshore drift is the movement of sand and shingle along a beach by waves that arrive at an angle.

entities.name: Sea breeze
entities.fact: A sea breeze is a cool wind that blows from the sea to the land during the day, as the land warms faster than the water.

entities.name: Internal wave
entities.fact: Internal waves travel along boundaries between layers of different density deep within the ocean, and they can be hundreds of metres high.

entities.name: Seiche
entities.fact: A seiche is a standing wave that sloshes back and forth in an enclosed or semi-enclosed body of water, such as a bay or lake.

entities.name: Dead zone
entities.fact: A dead zone is an area of the sea with too little oxygen for most marine life, often caused by fertiliser runoff.

entities.name: Marine snow
entities.fact: Marine snow is the steady fall of dead plankton, faecal pellets and other debris from the upper ocean to the deep seafloor.

entities.name: Ekman spiral
entities.fact: The Ekman spiral describes how water at successive depths is deflected by the Earth's rotation, so that the net transport is at right angles to the wind.

entities.name: Kelvin wave
entities.fact: Kelvin waves are huge, slow ocean waves that travel along the equator or the coast and help trigger El Nino.

entities.name: Rossby wave
entities.fact: Rossby waves are very large, slow waves in the ocean and atmosphere that arise from the rotation of the Earth.

entities.name: Meteotsunami
entities.fact: A meteotsunami is a tsunami-like wave caused by a rapid change in air pressure, such as from a storm front, rather than an earthquake.

entities.name: Sneaker wave
entities.fact: A sneaker wave is a surprisingly large wave that comes much farther up a beach than the ones before it and can sweep people off their feet.

entities.name: Brinicle
entities.fact: A brinicle is a hollow tube of ice that grows downward from sea ice, as very cold, salty brine sinks and freezes the water around it.

entities.name: Indian Ocean Dipole
entities.fact: The Indian Ocean Dipole is a swing in sea surface temperatures between the western and eastern Indian Ocean that affects rainfall around it.

entities.name: Pacific Decadal Oscillation
entities.fact: The Pacific Decadal Oscillation is a long-lived pattern of Pacific sea surface temperatures that shifts over decades.

entities.name: Sea smoke
entities.fact: Sea smoke is the wisps of fog that rise from relatively warm water when very cold air blows across it.

entities.name: Black smoker
entities.fact: A black smoker is a hydrothermal vent on the seabed that spews dark, mineral-rich water heated to hundreds of degrees Celsius.

entities.name: Milky sea
entities.fact: A milky sea is a rare sight in which the ocean glows white over a huge area at night, probably from luminous bacteria, and it can even be seen from satellites.

entities.name: Greenpeace
entities.fact: Greenpeace was founded in Vancouver in 1971 and campaigns against whaling, overfishing and ocean pollution, with ships such as the Rainbow Warrior.

entities.name: Sea Shepherd
entities.fact: Sea Shepherd was founded by Paul Watson in 1977 and takes direct action against illegal whaling, fishing and sealing.

entities.name: WWF
entities.fact: WWF is a global conservation charity founded in 1961 with a panda as its emblem, and it runs major marine programmes.

entities.name: Oceana
entities.fact: Oceana is an international ocean conservation group, founded in 2001, that campaigns on fishing, pollution and protecting marine habitats.

entities.name: Cousteau Society
entities.fact: The Cousteau Society was founded by Jacques Cousteau in 1973 to protect the oceans and educate the public.

entities.name: International Whaling Commission
entities.fact: The International Whaling Commission was set up in 1946 and agreed a moratorium on commercial whaling that took effect in 1986.

entities.name: United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea
entities.fact: UNCLOS, opened for signature in 1982, sets out the rules for the use of the oceans, including territorial waters and exclusive economic zones.

entities.name: CITES
aliases: Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species
entities.fact: CITES is a 1973 treaty regulating international trade in endangered species, including sharks, rays, seahorses and corals.

entities.name: MARPOL
aliases: International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships
entities.fact: MARPOL is the main international treaty against pollution from ships, adopted in 1973 and modified in 1978.

entities.name: Ocean Conservancy
entities.fact: Ocean Conservancy is an American non-profit group that organises the annual International Coastal Cleanup.

entities.name: Surfrider Foundation
entities.fact: The Surfrider Foundation was founded by surfers in California in 1984 to protect waves and beaches.

entities.name: Marine Conservation Society
entities.fact: The Marine Conservation Society is a British charity founded in 1983 that runs the Good Fish Guide and the Great British Beach Clean.

entities.name: Antarctic Treaty
entities.fact: The Antarctic Treaty of 1959 reserves Antarctica for peace and science and banned military activity south of 60 degrees south.

entities.name: Mission Blue
entities.fact: Mission Blue was founded by Sylvia Earle in 2009 and promotes marine protected areas it calls Hope Spots.

entities.name: The Ocean Cleanup
entities.fact: The Ocean Cleanup is a Dutch non-profit, founded by Boyan Slat in 2013, that develops systems to remove plastic from the oceans and rivers.

entities.name: 4ocean
entities.fact: 4ocean is a company founded in 2017 that pays crews to collect rubbish from oceans and coasts and sells bracelets made from recycled material.

entities.name: Whale and Dolphin Conservation
entities.fact: Whale and Dolphin Conservation is a charity that campaigns to protect whales and dolphins, and it is against keeping them in captivity.

entities.name: OSPAR Convention
entities.fact: The OSPAR Convention of 1992 protects the marine environment of the north-east Atlantic.

entities.name: CCAMLR
aliases: Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources
entities.fact: CCAMLR, established in 1982 and based in Hobart, manages the fishing of krill and other marine life in the Southern Ocean.

entities.name: HELCOM
entities.fact: HELCOM is the governing body of the Helsinki Convention, which protects the marine environment of the Baltic Sea.

entities.name: London Convention
aliases: London Convention on the Prevention of Marine Pollution by Dumping of Wastes
entities.fact: The London Convention of 1972 was an early treaty restricting the dumping of wastes at sea.

entities.name: High Seas Treaty
aliases: Agreement on Biodiversity Beyond National Jurisdiction
entities.fact: The High Seas Treaty, adopted at the United Nations in 2023, provides for protecting marine life in waters beyond any country's control.

entities.name: International Seabed Authority
entities.fact: The International Seabed Authority, based in Kingston, Jamaica, regulates mineral activities on the seabed beyond national waters.

entities.name: ICCAT
aliases: International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas
entities.fact: ICCAT is the commission formed in 1969 to manage tuna and tuna-like fish in the Atlantic Ocean.

entities.name: Marine Stewardship Council
entities.fact: The Marine Stewardship Council runs a certification scheme that labels sustainably caught wild fish with a blue tick.

entities.name: Reef Check
entities.fact: Reef Check is a volunteer-led programme in which trained divers survey coral reefs around the world to track their health.

entities.name: Project AWARE
entities.fact: Project AWARE is a non-profit working with the scuba diving community to protect the ocean, with a focus on marine debris and sharks.

entities.name: Coral Triangle Initiative
entities.fact: The Coral Triangle Initiative of 2009 is a partnership of six countries, including Indonesia and the Philippines, to protect the Coral Triangle's reefs and fisheries.

entities.name: Barcelona Convention
aliases: Convention for the Protection of the Mediterranean Sea
entities.fact: The Barcelona Convention of 1976 is the regional treaty for protecting the Mediterranean Sea from pollution.

entities.name: NASCO
entities.fact: NASCO, based in Edinburgh, is an intergovernmental body created in 1984 to conserve wild Atlantic salmon.

entities.name: International Pacific Halibut Commission
entities.fact: The International Pacific Halibut Commission, founded by the United States and Canada in 1923, manages halibut stocks in the north-eastern Pacific.

entities.name: Western and Central Pacific Fisheries Commission
entities.fact: The Western and Central Pacific Fisheries Commission, established by a 2000 convention, manages tuna fisheries across a vast area of the Pacific.

entities.name: Shark Trust
entities.fact: The Shark Trust is a British charity founded in 1997 that works for the conservation of sharks and rays.

entities.name: Oceanic Preservation Society
entities.fact: The Oceanic Preservation Society, led by Louie Psihoyos, made the Oscar-winning documentary The Cove about dolphin hunting in Japan.

entities.name: Blue Marine Foundation
entities.fact: The Blue Marine Foundation is a British charity set up in 2010 that campaigns for large marine protected areas.

entities.name: Coral Restoration Foundation
entities.fact: The Coral Restoration Foundation, based in Key Largo, Florida, grows coral in underwater nurseries and plants it back onto damaged reefs.

entities.name: Ocean Alliance
entities.fact: Ocean Alliance is a whale research and conservation group founded by Roger Payne, who helped to discover that humpbacks sing.

entities.name: Sea Legacy
entities.fact: Sea Legacy is a conservation group founded by photographers Paul Nicklen and Cristina Mittermeier that uses imagery to promote ocean protection.

entities.name: Sustainable Fisheries Partnership
entities.fact: The Sustainable Fisheries Partnership works with the seafood industry to improve how fisheries are managed.

entities.name: Marine Mammal Commission
entities.fact: The Marine Mammal Commission is an independent United States agency created by the Marine Mammal Protection Act of 1972.

entities.name: Madrid Protocol
aliases: Protocol on Environmental Protection to the Antarctic Treaty
entities.fact: The Madrid Protocol of 1991 designates Antarctica a natural reserve and bans mining there.

entities.name: Cartagena Convention
aliases: Convention for the Protection and Development of the Marine Environment of the Wider Caribbean Region
entities.fact: The Cartagena Convention of 1983 is the regional treaty for protecting the marine environment of the wider Caribbean.

entities.name: International Convention for the Regulation of Whaling
entities.fact: The International Convention for the Regulation of Whaling, signed in Washington in 1946, created the International Whaling Commission.

entities.name: Convention for the Conservation of Antarctic Seals
entities.fact: The 1972 Convention for the Conservation of Antarctic Seals limits the killing of seals south of 60 degrees south, and no commercial sealing has been carried out under it.

entities.name: Surfing
entities.fact: Surfing is riding waves on a board, and it developed over centuries among the Polynesians of the Pacific.

entities.name: Swimming
entities.fact: Swimming in the sea is one of the oldest water sports, and open-water swimming events cover distances from a few hundred metres to marathon crossings.

entities.name: Sailing
entities.fact: Sailing uses wind in sails to move a boat across the water, in recreation and in racing.

entities.name: Scuba diving
entities.fact: Scuba diving uses a self-contained breathing apparatus, a name that stands for self-contained underwater breathing apparatus, to explore underwater.

entities.name: Snorkelling
entities.fact: Snorkelling is swimming at the surface with a mask and a breathing tube to watch marine life below.

entities.name: Kayaking
entities.fact: Kayaking uses a double-bladed paddle to move a covered boat, a design that began with Arctic peoples.

entities.name: Water polo
entities.fact: Water polo is a team sport played in a pool in which two teams try to score by throwing a ball into the opposing goal, and it has been an Olympic sport since 1900.

entities.name: Windsurfing
entities.fact: Windsurfing combines surfing with sailing, using a board with a hand-held sail.

entities.name: Kitesurfing
entities.fact: Kitesurfing uses a large controllable kite to pull a rider on a board across the water.

entities.name: Stand-up paddleboarding
entities.fact: Stand-up paddleboarding is riding a long board while standing and using a single-bladed paddle, a sport that spread from Hawaii.

entities.name: Canoeing
entities.fact: Canoeing is paddling a canoe with a single-bladed paddle, and it has been an Olympic sport since 1936.

entities.name: Rowing
entities.fact: Rowing propels a boat using oars, and ocean rowers cross entire oceans in small boats.

entities.name: Water skiing
entities.fact: Water skiing is being towed behind a boat on skis, an idea first tried in 1922 by Ralph Samuelson in Minnesota.

entities.name: Wakeboarding
entities.fact: Wakeboarding is riding a board across the water while towed behind a boat, using its wake to jump.

entities.name: Bodyboarding
entities.fact: Bodyboarding is riding waves lying down on a short, foam board.

entities.name: Jet skiing
entities.fact: Jet skiing is riding a small, motorised personal watercraft across the water.

entities.name: Parasailing
entities.fact: Parasailing is a sport in which a person is towed behind a boat while attached to a parachute-like canopy.

entities.name: Spearfishing
entities.fact: Spearfishing is hunting fish underwater with a speargun or pole spear, usually while free-diving.

entities.name: Sea fishing
entities.fact: Sea fishing as a sport includes angling from shore and from boats for species such as marlin and tuna.

entities.name: Open water swimming
entities.fact: Open water swimming takes place in the sea, rivers or lakes rather than in a pool, and it is an Olympic event over ten kilometres.

entities.name: Skimboarding
entities.fact: Skimboarding is riding a thin board that is thrown onto the thin sheet of water at the shoreline, then sliding on to catch a wave.

entities.name: Bodysurfing
entities.fact: Bodysurfing is riding a wave without a board, using only the body.

entities.name: Outrigger canoe racing
entities.fact: Outrigger canoe racing uses long canoes with a float attached on one side, a sport popular across Polynesia and especially in Hawaii and Tahiti.

entities.name: Dragon boat racing
entities.fact: Dragon boat racing is a team paddling sport using long boats with dragon heads and tails, which began in China.

entities.name: Kneeboarding
entities.fact: Kneeboarding is being towed behind a boat while kneeling on a board.

entities.name: Flyboarding
entities.fact: Flyboarding uses a board with jets of water, attached by a hose to a personal watercraft, to lift the rider into the air.

entities.name: Windfoiling
entities.fact: Windfoiling is windsurfing on a board with a hydrofoil, which lifts the board clear of the water at speed.

entities.name: Wingfoiling
entities.fact: Wingfoiling is a sport in which the rider holds a hand-held inflatable wing and rides a hydrofoil board.

entities.name: Surf lifesaving
entities.fact: Surf lifesaving sport grew from the beach rescue clubs of Australia and tests skills such as swimming, board paddling and rescue.

entities.name: Big wave surfing
entities.fact: Big wave surfing is riding waves that reach several metres, such as those at Nazare in Portugal and Mavericks in California.

entities.name: Cliff diving
entities.fact: Cliff diving is diving into the sea from high rocks or platforms, and elite competitors dive from over twenty metres.

entities.name: Pilot gig racing
entities.fact: Pilot gig racing is a rowing sport using six-oared Cornish pilot gigs, and the world championships are held at the Isles of Scilly.

entities.name: Tow-in surfing
entities.fact: Tow-in surfing uses a personal watercraft to tow surfers into waves that are too big and fast to paddle into.

entities.name: No-limits freediving
entities.fact: No-limits freediving is diving as deep as possible on one breath using a weighted sled to descend and a lift bag to ascend.

entities.name: Dinghy racing
entities.fact: Dinghy racing is a form of sailing in small, open boats, which are raced in classes such as Laser, Optimist and Finn.

entities.name: Surf ski paddling
entities.fact: Surf ski paddling uses a long, narrow sit-on-top kayak to race in open sea and ocean swells.

entities.name: Wreck diving
entities.fact: Wreck diving is scuba diving to explore sunken ships and aircraft.

entities.name: Technical diving
entities.fact: Technical diving is scuba diving beyond the usual recreational limits, using special gas mixtures and staged decompression.

entities.name: Offshore powerboat racing
entities.fact: Offshore powerboat racing is a high-speed race in powerful boats over open sea courses.

entities.name: Ocean rowing
entities.fact: Ocean rowing is crossing an ocean in a rowing boat, and hundreds of people have rowed across the Atlantic.

entities.name: Marathon swimming
entities.fact: Marathon swimming is open water swimming over very long distances, such as crossing the English Channel.

entities.name: Match racing
entities.fact: Match racing is a form of sailing in which two boats race directly against each other, as in the America's Cup.

entities.name: Surf kayaking
entities.fact: Surf kayaking is riding ocean waves in a kayak.

entities.name: Formula Kite
entities.fact: Formula Kite is a racing class of kitesurfing on hydrofoil boards, and it made its debut at the Paris 2024 Olympics.

entities.name: Coasteering
entities.fact: Coasteering is travelling along a rocky coastline by climbing, scrambling, swimming and jumping into the sea, and the sport began in Wales.
